title: Clarifying uses and misuses of Global Fishing Watch fishing data
content:
Abstract
The study by Hintzen et al. compared fishing events from Global Fishing Watch’s (GFW) Application Programming Interface (API) with gear deployment observations from self-sampling programmes on board two pelagic trawling fleets in the Northeast Atlantic Ocean. They found strong agreement in fishing locations and differences in the number of events and durations, concluding that GFW fishing events over-predict effort for these fleets. GFW’s general fishing model was trained to predict fishing-related activity, including searching, setting, hauling, and soaking gear, among others, to produce a spatial distribution of apparent fishing activity at a global level across all fishing gears. The fishing events derived from these predictions should therefore not be interpreted to represent all fishery-specific measures of effort, or in this case, individual hauls in these two pelagic fisheries. In this paper, we described GFW’s general fishing model and the publicly available apparent fishing datasets shared on our platforms. We also reviewed the studies mentioned in Hintzen et al., which they suggested may be affected by biases in the GFW general fishing model. Our review indicated that most of the mentioned studies used GFW fishing data to analyse the spatial distribution of fishing, which was shown by Hintzen et al. to be accurate. We agree with Hintzen et al. that closer collaboration with fishing experts and comparisons with high-quality logbook or observer data are essential for improving GFW or other similar fishing activity data. Furthermore, we advocate for the development and publication of gear-specific fishing models to enhance the applicability of such datasets.
